title: K-B-D

segments.voice: Yesterday, children and builders: banayich read as bonayich, the kid on the rug laying stones for peace. Your line was children are builders. Who got your sentence? Today, a root you can feel in your arms. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-four.

Some people leave a meeting and nobody notices the chair is empty. Others step out for a minute and the whole room goes a little off balance, as if something heavy has been lifted off the table. English has a way of saying it: she carries weight, his word carries weight. We talk about importance as if it had a mass you could put on a scale. Hebrew does more than talk that way. It builds the idea into a root. The same three letters that mean heavy also mean honor. Kaf, vet, dalet: K-B-D.
screen: `THE ROOM GOES OFF BALANCE.` → `HIS WORD CARRIES WEIGHT.` → `K-B-D: HEAVY, AND HONOR.`

segments.voice: Turn K-B-D four ways. First, heavy. Israel is fighting Amalek, and Moses stands on a hill with his hands raised. While they're up, Israel prevails; when they drop, Amalek does. Then the text says, "But Moses' hands were heavy." The word is from this root: kaved, heavy. So Aaron and Hur put a stone under him to sit on, and they hold up his hands, one on each side, until the sun goes down. Second, honor. From the commandments: "Honour thy father and thy mother." Honor there is kabed, from the very same letters. To honor a parent, in the root's own picture, is to treat them as heavy: not light, not easy to brush aside. Third, glory. When Moses goes up Sinai, the text says "the glory of the LORD abode upon mount Sinai," and a cloud covers the mountain. Glory there is kavod. Presence that settles, that has weight, that doesn't drift off. Fourth, the twist, from Pirkei Avot. Ben Zoma asks: who is honored? And he answers: the one who honors other people. You don't get weight by demanding it. You get it by giving it. Put the four together. A tired man's arms. A parent at the table. A cloud on a mountain. A sage's question. Honor, in Hebrew, isn't a title or a medal. It's a matter of how much someone weighs to you. Whether their words land, or blow away.
screen: `HEAVY: MOSES' HANDS.` · `HONOR: THY FATHER AND THY MOTHER.` · `GLORY: THE CLOUD ON SINAI.` · `WHO IS HONORED? WHO HONORS OTHERS.` · then, large: `כָּבוֹד`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give someone weight. Settle, and breathe. Let your hands rest heavy in your lap, and notice their weight. Now bring to mind someone whose words you tend to skim: a parent, a coworker, an older neighbor who tells the same story twice. Recall one thing they said lately, and this time let it land. Let it weigh what it weighs. What were they really telling you? Decide one way you could treat their words as heavy today. If you pray, you can hold them in the quiet. The bell holds the time.
K-B-D. Kaf, vet, dalet: the root of kaved, heavy, and kavod, honor and glory. To honor is to give weight. Today's word.
Your line: honor is weight. Today, when that person speaks, put your phone down, turn toward them, and let their words land before you answer. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: Kibbud av va'em, honoring father and mother, is a commandment Jews study and practice in detail; and the word kavod, honor, is used in daily Jewish life for the respect owed to every person.

original.note: Hebrew: honor, glory; from the root K-B-D, heavy.

trapdoor: what you thought: honor is a title or a medal.
what it means: in Hebrew, kavod, honor, shares its root with kaved, heavy.
what a scholar hears: the same root names Moses' heavy hands, the command to honor parents, and God's glory on Sinai.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Exodus 17:12, 20:12 and 24:16 as quoted.
Root claims: kaved (heavy, Exodus 17:12 kevedim), kabed (Exodus 20:12) and kavod (Exodus 24:16) all from K-B-D, as the outline states. Confirm.
Avot 4:1 (Ben Zoma) paraphrased: 'who is honored? one who honors others.' Confirm.
Exodus 24:16: the cloud is mentioned in 24:15-16; framing 'a cloud covers the mountain' is from the passage.
